summary: Describes a clock service offered by DCNET hosts, meant for clock synchronization and measuring one-way delay with cooperating hosts. It used timestamp messages from the proposed ICMP, and briefly also GGP echo messages for compatibility. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers on a network can ask another computer what time it is, a bit like checking a friend's watch to set your own. This memo explains how one network offered that.

subtitle: Allow computers on the network to ask each other what time it is, for clock synchronization and delay measurement

tldr.problem: Computers on the network need synchronized clocks for accurate measurement and logging, but existing methods require direct user access to timing protocols that operating systems like TOPS-20 did not expose.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Clock Service uses either ICMP Timestamp messages or GGP Echo messages, embedding three timestamps in a datagram. A sender fills all three with its local time; the receiver records when it arrives and when it sends the reply back. This allows both one-way delay and roundtrip measurement.
tldr.outcome: DCNET hosts and gateways offer clock synchronization with the accuracy of ICMP or GGP datagrams, which bypass normal queueing and provide stable timing references.

today: RFC 778 is Historic status from April 1981. It describes an early approach to network clock synchronization that has been superseded by more advanced protocols like NTP.

sections.title: Clock Synchronization on DCNET
sections.content:
All DCNET hosts provide an Internet Clock Service (ICS) intended for clock synchronization and measuring network delay with cooperating hosts. The service uses the Timestamp and Timestamp Reply messages of the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), or for compatibility with existing systems, the Echo and Echo Reply messages of the Gateway-Gateway Protocol (GGP).

ICMP and GGP datagrams bypass normal user-level queueing in gateways and hosts, making them useful as accurate time references more stable than ordinary data traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer asks another computer for the time, the answer comes through special fast messages that skip the normal wait, so the time is more accurate.

sections.title: The Clock Service Datagram
sections.content:
An ICS datagram carries a type (8 for GGP Echo or 13 for ICMP Timestamp), a code field (zero), a sequence number, and three 32-bit timestamp fields. The sender fills all three timestamps with its local time in milliseconds from midnight UTC before sending.

The receiving host or gateway records the arrival time in the receive timestamp field and the departure time in the transmit timestamp field, then reverses the type to indicate a reply (0 for GGP Echo Reply, 14 for ICMP Timestamp Reply). The datagram is 36 octets inclusive of the 20-octet IP header. Roundtrip delay (t4 - t3) plus (t2 - t1) yields the total time, while one-way delays can be measured if both endpoints participate.
sections.plainLanguage: The message holds three times: when sent, when received, and when sent back. From these, you can figure out how long the message took to travel each way.

sections.title: Using the Clock Service
sections.content: The COMSAT-WWV virtual host at internet address [29,0,9,2] is connected to a Spectracom radio clock synchronized to WWVB, providing accurate time to within a millisecond. Users can retrieve current clock offsets and NBS time status by connecting via Telnet to COMSAT-GAT at [29,0,1,2] and sending commands SET HOST HOST (to see offsets) and SET WWV SHOW (to see radio clock status). Roundtrip delay to COMSAT-GAT from BBN Gateway is typically 550 milliseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer on the network has a super-accurate clock radio. You can ask it what time it is, and it tells you what corrections each computer needs.

references.text: Postel, J., "Internet Control Message Protocol", RFC 777, USC/Information Sciences Institute, April 1981.
